name: Feature Stores
title: Feature Stores
answer: A feature store is a managed set of tables of model input values, computed once and served identically to training and to production, which prevents a model from being trained on one definition of a value and run on another. It sits between the systems that hold raw data, such as a warehouse or an event stream, and the systems that consume model inputs, such as a training pipeline or an online service. The scope covers both the offline side, where large historical tables are assembled for training, and the online side, where a small number of values must be returned in milliseconds for a single request. Feature stores are most common where several models share the same inputs, or where a value such as a customer's recent activity must mean the same thing in both places.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A feature store runs on two storage layers that are kept in step. The offline layer is usually a warehouse or lakehouse table format, holding the full history of each feature with timestamps so that a training set can be rebuilt as of any past moment. The online layer is a low latency key value store, often backed by a cache or an in memory database, holding only the latest value per entity. A materialization job moves computed features from the offline layer to the online layer on a schedule or on a stream. Because the site's own pages are built from a PostgreSQL database, it is worth noting that many feature stores use PostgreSQL or a similar relational engine for metadata, definitions and lineage, even when the feature values themselves live elsewhere.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a definition: a named feature, its entity key, its source tables and the transformation that produces it. Teams write that transformation once, in SQL or in a dataframe framework, and the store applies the same logic to historical data for training and to fresh data for serving. Point in time joins are the central technique, matching each training row to the feature values that were actually known at that moment, which avoids leaking future information into the model. Backfills recompute a feature over past data when its definition changes. Monitoring then compares the distribution of values seen in training with what arrives in production, so that drift or a broken upstream job is caught before it degrades a model.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance in a feature store is mostly about ownership and traceability. Each feature has an owner, a description, a data type and a documented source, so that a model's inputs can be traced back to the tables and jobs that produced them. Access controls decide who may read a feature, since some inputs are derived from personal or regulated data, and the same controls usually apply to the offline and online copies. Retention rules matter because the online layer holds current values while the offline layer may hold years of history. Lineage records which models consume which features, so that a change to a definition can be assessed before it ships, and so that a feature can be deprecated without silently breaking a model in production.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward fewer separate systems and more shared definitions. Feature platforms are converging with the warehouse, with the semantic layer and with model context tooling, so that a value defined once can be reached by a training job, an online service and an agent alike. Streaming materialization is becoming more common, narrowing the gap between a value being computed and a value being served. The site currently tracks 2,598 active Model Context Protocol servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses, a sign of how much of this work now runs through standard interfaces rather than bespoke connectors. The open questions are less about storage and more about consistency, cost of keeping two copies, and how much of the definition layer can be automated.
